units.translation: which expression Longinus also notes in this fragment, On the Sublime 3, 1, with the words: οὐ τραγικὰ ἔτι ταῦτα, ἀλλὰ παρατράγῳδα [these are no longer tragic, but para-tragic] τεθόλωται γὰρ τῇ φράσει καὶ τεθορύβηται ταῖς φαντασίαις μᾶλλον ἢ δεδείνωται [for it is muddied in its diction and confused in its imagery rather than made terrible].
has been dashed to the ground
a vessel encircled by the coils of serpents
these are no longer tragic, but para-tragic; for it is muddied in its diction and confused in its imagery rather than made terrible
Θανόντος ἐν πλεκταῖσι καὶ [of the dead man in the coils and]
in the coils of a dread viper
of the dead man in the coils and
Ἀλλ᾽ ἡ δόλον τιν᾽, ὦ ξέν᾽, ἀμφ᾽ ἐμοὶ [But she, some trick, O stranger, around me]
the Egyptians are clever at weaving schemes
But she, some trick, O stranger, around me

where in most copies πνευμόνων [lungs], which forms the grammarians rightly distinguish thus: πλεύμων [lung] is Attic, πνεύμων [lung], which the scribes very often introduced, is assigned to the common dialect; on which I have spoken in Thes. vol. 6 p. 1261.
the sword near the lungs pierces through with sharp point
there is one example in Aeschylus
he cast around the sides the arm-straps
what pain creeps under my sides?
Όμοσπλάγχνων τε [and of the same entrails]
of the sides of a cauldron
For thus Jacobitz corrected to πληρώμασιν [fillings].
whatever you boil in the sides of a hollow dish
For thus Jacobitz corrected to πληρώμασιν [fillings]
they sail as each had been assigned
he sailed on the breeze of the giant Zephyrus
they sailed thus with favorable wrath
the remaining cases are taken partly from this form, partly from the unused nominative πλέος [full], as the examples to be cited below and others collected in Thes. vol. 6 p. 1191 show
Ἀεί γε δὴ νηλής σὺ καὶ θράσους [Always indeed you are pitiless and full of boldness]
Ναύταισι θερμοῖς καὶ πανουργίας [to hot sailors and of wickedness]
Thus I corrected what is in M: πανουργίαι τινί [with some wickedness].
The nominative πλέῳ [full] is not found in Sophocles and Euripides; the dative πλέως [full] for πλέως [full] Meineke restored in Cratinus ap. Athen. 9 p. 410d.
Ἐμοὶ γὰρ ἤδη πάντα μὲν φόβου [For to me already all things are full of fear]
Always indeed you are pitiless and full of boldness
to hot sailors and of wickedness
